correctness.rationale: Independently averaged the actual, unsymmetrized Fourier transform over each nonzero dual ray D, obtaining (q μ(D⊥)−1)/(q−1). Missing rays all have mean t=(qa−1)/(q−1), where a is the origin atom, and the aggregate mean on selected rays is y=[1+(k−1)t]/k, using Σ_j μ(L_j)=1+(k−1)a and the equal ray sizes. The optimum over t∈[−1/(q−1),1] is unique: -t descends and y strictly ascends until their crossing, or the domain truncates before the crossing. A constant line weight attains each fixed-mass bound, so all optimizers must have the claimed a. At q≤2k, including the boundary, the selected aggregate mean and the missing means are ± the bound; a disk average at the endpoint ±m requires every value to equal that endpoint, by the real-part inequality. Thus every coefficient including the zero one is determined and Fourier inversion gives outright uniqueness with no reversibility hypothesis. At q>2k selected frequencies still saturate and are fixed; omitted ones have strict slack for the canonical optimizer. In F₇ on the two axes and diagonal, an odd function g supported at ±1 with values ±1 produces f=(g,g,−g) along the three punctured lines. Its total mass is zero and its transform is ĝ(u)+ĝ(v)−ĝ(u+v), which vanishes on the three selected dual lines. Since ||f||₁=6, adding ε f for 0<|ε|<1/108 is feasible from the uniform nonzero weights 1/18 and leaves every omitted magnitude strictly below 2/9 (the original magnitude is 1/6). Both distinct masses attain the bound, and the perturbation is not even.

evidence: Jafarizadeh's indexed abstract specifically states optimal transition probabilities assign identical weights to edges within the same adjacency relation of association-scheme networks. The loopless pencil graph has degree d=k(q−1) and nonconstant adjacency eigenvalues q−k and −k, by orthogonality. A real undirected regular graph with these two nonconstant eigenvalues is strongly regular: A² is a linear combination of I, A, and the all-ones matrix by spectral multiplication. Hence I, A, and the complement adjacency form its two-class symmetric association scheme.
